entries.text: HbA1c at or above this value is in the diabetes range, where the assay is quality-assured and no validity caveat holds
entries.source: WHO · Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation · 2011 (WHO/NMH/CHP/CPM/11.1)

x.quote: HbA1c can be used as a diagnostic test for diabetes providing that stringent quality assurance tests are in place and assays are standardised to criteria aligned to the international reference values [...] An HbA1c of 6.5% is recommended as the cut point for diagnosing diabetes. A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests.
x.note: WHO 2011 and HEARTS-D Table 3 print '6.5%' as a cut point with no operator; 'at or above' is explicit only in ADA Table 2.1. HEARTS-D adds that plasma glucose is preferred in people with symptoms.

verification.note: 6.5% confirmed as the WHO 2011 cut point. Neither WHO 2011 nor HEARTS-D Table 3 ('HbA1c*** | 6.5% (48 mmol/mol)') prints an operator; 'at or above' is the ordinary reading of 'cut point' and is explicit only in the ADA claim, which I did not open. HEARTS-D footnote to the HbA1c row: 'Plasma glucose is preferred in people with symptoms who are suspected of having type 1 diabetes.'

entries.text: 1-hour plasma glucose after 75 g at or above this value defines type 2 diabetes in the IDF 2024 position statement; needs a repeat test
entries.source: IDF · Bergman M, Manco M, Satman I, et al. International Diabetes Federation Position Statement on the 1-hour post-load plasma glucose for the diagnosis of intermediate hyperglycaemia and type 2 diabetes. Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2024;209:111589 · 2024

x.quote: People with a 1-h PG ≥ 155 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L) are considered to have IH and should be prescribed lifestyle intervention and referred to a diabetes prevention program. People with a 1-h PG ≥ 209 mg/dL (11.6 mmol/L) are considered to have T2D and should have a repeat test to confirm the diagnosis of T2D
x.conflicts: Not adopted by WHO or ADA (A3-20). IDF prints the mg/dL equivalent as 209 in the position statement and 210 in its 2025 recommendations.

verification.note: Value, operator (>=), unit and attribution (IDF position statement, Bergman et al., Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2024) match; abstract only was read. Minor mg/dL discrepancy between IDF documents: the IDF Global Clinical Practice Recommendations 2025 (p. 25) print 'a 1 h PG ≥11.6 mmol/L (210 mg/dL) for diagnosing T2DM', versus 209 mg/dL in the position statement. The mmol/L value is the same in both. The 2025 document does not restate the repeat-test requirement.
verification.foundQuote: People with a 1-h PG ≥ 209 mg/dL (11.6 mmol/L) are considered to have T2D and should have a repeat test to confirm the diagnosis of T2D

entries.text: Asymptomatic: one abnormal result is not a diagnosis. Repeat, preferably the same test, on a subsequent day.

verification.note: Also read in WHO 2011 (NBK304271): 'The diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic person should not be made on the basis of a single abnormal plasma glucose or HbA1c value.' and in WHO 1999 section 2.2.1: 'The diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic subject should never be made on the basis of a single abnormal blood glucose value.'

entries.text: Hyperglycaemia found at TB diagnosis: reassess glycaemic status after
entries.source: WHO · WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 6: tuberculosis and comorbidities, third edition (diabetes chapter; ISBN 9789240103276; announced 7 Feb 2025) · 2025 (3rd ed. handbook)

x.quote: Glucose levels can be elevated at the time of TB diagnosis due to stress or TB infection-related hyperglycaemia. … It is therefore critical to reassess the glycaemic status after 1 month as part of standard diabetes management.

verification.note: The '1 month' figure is verbatim in section 4.1: 'It is therefore critical to reassess the glycaemic status after 1 month as part of standard diabetes management.' Earlier in the same passage: 'glucose levels can be elevated at the time of TB diagnosis due to stress or TB infection-related hyperglycaemia. Infection-related hyperglycaemia tends to decrease during TB treatment.' and 'diabetes management should be based on the level of glycaemia, regardless of whether the hyperglycaemia might be transient or not.' Qualifiers the entry lacks: (1) the handbook does not say what the month is counted from (it reads as one month after the hyperglycaemia is found and management starts); (2) the reassessment is framed as part of standard diabetes management, i.e. treatment is started on the glucose level and then reviewed, not withheld for a month; (3) there is a second requirement, that testing is offered before TB treatment ends. The fetch tool declined to reproduce the whole section, so the passage was read in excerpts; the three consecutive sentences above were returned as one block. Edition and year are not shown on the page.
verification.foundQuote: If the hyperglycaemia is in fact transient, the treatment may not be continued at later follow-up appointments, according to glycaemic values. It is therefore critical to reassess the glycaemic status after 1 month as part of standard diabetes management. People with TB and newly diagnosed hyperglycaemia should be advised about the importance of reassessment of glycaemic status, and the TB care provider should ensure that testing is offered before TB treatment ends, either at the facility or through referral to a facility where diabetes care is provided.

entries.text: A single normal fasting glucose or HbA1c is a weak negative in a high-risk African adult: each misses a third or more of OGTT-defined diabetes. The 2-hour OGTT is the most sensitive test.

x.quote: A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests.
x.note: A synthesis of four sources, not a quotation. Against the OGTT: HbA1c sensitivity 57.7% (Chivese, pooled African studies) and 69.8% (Kasujja, eastern Uganda); fasting glucose 44.3% (Baye) and 62.6% (Kasujja).

verification.note: A synthesis, not a quotation, and correctly labelled as such. The component numbers were read at the three other-claim URLs. 'A third or more' holds for Chivese (HbA1c misses about 42%) and Baye (FPG misses 44% or more; the abstract's 44.3% sensitivity and '44.4% missed' do not add up, so quote one of them, not both), and for FPG in Kasujja (about 37%). Kasujja's HbA1c sensitivity of 69.8% means about 30% missed, just under a third, with a wide interval. Baye reports FPG only, not HbA1c. OpenAlex lists Chivese as 2021, not 2022. 'The 2-hour OGTT is the most sensitive test' is true by construction in these studies (the OGTT is the reference standard); none of the passages I read states it as a finding. ADA Section 2 not opened.

entries.text: Anything that shortens red-cell survival (haemolysis, recovery from blood loss) falsely LOWERS HbA1c whatever the assay. After transfusion, in sickle cell disease and with malaria the result is unreliable in a direction that cannot be predicted: use glucose.
entries.source: OTHER · NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results · NGSP web page, last updated 23 June 2026 as displayed

x.quote: Any condition that shortens erythrocyte survival or decreases mean erythrocyte age (e.g., recovery from acute blood loss ...) will falsely lower HbA1c test results regardless of the assay method ... HbA1c results from patients with HbSS, HbCC, and HbSC must be interpreted with caution
x.note: NGSP states the direction only for shortened red-cell survival. It gives none for transfusion or homozygous variants ('interpreted with caution'), and does not mention malaria; WHO 2011 lists malaria without a direction.

verification.note: The principle (shortened red-cell survival falsely lowers HbA1c regardless of assay method) is confirmed, with NGSP examples "recovery from acute blood loss, hemolytic anemia". But the entry's list goes beyond what the sources say: (1) transfusion: NGSP gives no direction; it appears only as a reason for caution in HbSS/HbCC/HbSC; (2) HbSS and HbSC: NGSP says "must be interpreted with caution", direction not stated (and ADA 2026 Section 6 says A1C cannot be measured at all in HbSS); (3) malaria: not mentioned on the NGSP page. Malaria appears in WHO 2011 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK304271/): "The most common important factors worldwide affecting HbA1c levels are haemoglobinopathies (depending on the assay employed), certain anaemias, and disorders associated with accelerated red cell turnover such as malaria", again without a stated direction. WHO 2011 Annex 1 lists under Decreased HbA1c "decreased erythrocyte life span: haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis or drugs"; malaria and transfusion are not in that table. Reword so that transfusion, HbSS/HbSC and malaria are "unreliable, interpret with caution / use glucose" rather than "falsely lowers".

entries.text: Always consider active Charcot foot in a person with diabetes, neuropathy and intact skin whose foot is warmer, swollen and/or red compared with the other foot. Start knee-high offloading promptly while it is investigated (IWGDF). NICE: refer within 1 working day.

x.quote: Always consider active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in a person with diabetes mellitus, neuropathy and intact skin when there are clinical findings of an increase in temperature, oedema, and/or redness of the foot, compared to the contralateral foot.

verification.note: Three qualifiers. (1) IWGDF says 'and/or': any one of warmth, oedema or redness is enough to consider Charcot, not all three as 'warm, swollen, red' implies; and the wording is 'always consider', not 'is Charcot until shown otherwise'. (2) 'Refer' is not an IWGDF Charcot recommendation (the fetch found none); it comes from NICE NG19 1.7.3: 'refer the person within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service for triage within 1 further working day. Offer non-weight-bearing treatment'. (3) 'No skin-temperature threshold is endorsed' is true of IWGDF for DIAGNOSIS, but NICE NG19 1.7.7 does use a number for RESOLUTION: 'Acute Charcot arthropathy is likely to resolve when there is a sustained temperature difference of less than 2 degrees between both feet'.

Recommendation 5: Initiate knee high immobilization/offloading promptly while further diagnostic studies are performed to confirm or rule out active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy (CNO), when active CNO is suspected. ... An increase in skin temperature of 2° Celsius or 4° Fahrenheit (which is actually 2.2°C) of the involved foot compared to the same location on the uninvolved foot has been used as a diagnostic threshold for active CNO in several publications. ... entries.text: WHO primary-care ladder for type 2 diabetes: diet and physical activity; then metformin; then add a sulfonylurea (gliclazide preferred); then human insulin or referral. A DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor or thiazolidinedione only if insulin is unsuitable. Review 3 months after each step.
entries.source: WHO · Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes (HEARTS-D) · 2020 (WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1)

x.section: Section 'Control of blood glucose levels (glycaemia)' (pp.14-15); Fig. 1 (p.16); Fig. 2 (p.25)
x.quote: Metformin does not cause weight gain or hypoglycaemia and is the recommended initial treatment [...] Add a second-generation sulfonylurea (preferably gliclazide) to metformin [...] Refer for insulin treatment or add human insulin to oral medication [...] If insulin is unsuitable, a DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT-2 inhibitor or a thiazolidinedione (TZD) may be added
x.note: 'Review 3 months after each step' is Fig. 2's wording.
x.conflicts: When metformin starts: HEARTS-D body text and Fig. 1 say after diet and physical activity have not achieved control; Fig. 2 (the WHO PEN protocol) starts it at diagnosis alongside them. Before insulin: a Fig. 2 footnote allows a DPP-4 inhibitor, an SGLT2 inhibitor or pioglitazone 'if they are more affordable than insulin', which is wider than 'only if insulin is unsuitable'.

verification.note: The ladder order is confirmed by the body text (pp.14-15). Three qualifiers the entry lacks. (1) When metformin starts: the body text and Fig. 1 make metformin conditional ('for people who do not achieve the desired glycaemic control with diet and physical activity'; 'IF goal not achieved BEGIN METFORMIN'), but Fig. 2, the WHO-PEN-derived protocol on p.25, starts metformin at diagnosis together with counselling ('BEGIN METFORMIN [dose omitted] once daily. Counsel on diet and physical activity and adherence at ALL visits', no 'if goal not achieved'). The document carries both; the catalogue should say which it follows. (2) 'Review 3 months after each step' holds for Fig. 2 only; Fig. 1 also prints 'REVIEW in 3–5 days', 'REVIEW in 2–3 months' and 'REVIEW IN 1 MONTH', whose positions I could not read. (3) Fig. 2 footnote: 'If they are more affordable than insulin, DPP4-inhibitors, SGLT2-inhibitors or pioglitazone can be used before insulin in cases of treatment failure with metformin and gliclazide', which is wider than 'only if insulin is unsuitable'. Fig. 1 also has a separate arm for severe hyperglycaemia that starts two medicines at once. WHO 2018 guideline (NBK532235) not opened. The WHO PEN training manual says 'Metformin is recommended as the first-line medicine in the treatment of diabetes. Sulfonylurea is recommended as the second-line treatment, and human insulin as the third-line treatment.' and, as relayed by the reader, its case studies prescribe metformin alongside lifestyle advice at diagnosis.
